title: Critical Thinking · Episode 1
chapters: Deduction, induction and abduction: three ways to reason
Why conspiracy theories feel so convincing

units.t: Critical Thinking. Episode one.
In this episode: Deduction, induction and abduction: three ways to reason, Correlation vs causation, How to spot misinformation and Why conspiracy theories feel so convincing.
Part one. Deduction, induction and abduction: three ways to reason.
Sherlock Holmes called it deduction, but he was usually doing something else.
Learn the three basic kinds of reasoning, and what each can and can't prove.
Holmes reads Watson.
In A Study in Scarlet, published in 1887, Sherlock Holmes shakes hands with Dr John Watson and says, ‘You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.’
Watson is astonished.
Holmes later explains his chain of thought.
Here was a gentleman of a medical type with a military air, so probably an army doctor.
His face was tanned but his wrists were pale, so he had recently come from the tropics.
He looked haggard and held his left arm stiffly, suggesting illness and an injury.
Where might an English army doctor recently have suffered such hardship?
Afghanistan.
Holmes called this the science of deduction.
Logicians would say he was mostly doing something different.
To see why, we need three kinds of reasoning.
Deduction: certainty.
Deduction moves from general statements to a conclusion that follows necessarily.
All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates is mortal.
If both starting statements, called premises, are true, the conclusion cannot be false.
That is deduction's great strength: certainty.
Its weakness is that the conclusion contains nothing that wasn't already packed inside the premises.
Deduction also depends completely on the premises being right.
An argument can be valid in structure and still reach a false conclusion if a premise is wrong: all birds can fly; penguins are birds; therefore penguins can fly.
Logicians call an argument ‘sound’ only when it is valid and its premises are actually true.
Induction: patterns.
Induction works the other way, from particular observations to general conclusions.
The sun has risen every morning in recorded history, so it will rise tomorrow.
Every swan Europeans had ever seen was white, so all swans must be white.
Most of our everyday knowledge, and much of science, rests on reasoning like this, and usually it serves us well.
But an inductive conclusion can always be overturned by new evidence.
In 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh and his crew saw black swans on a river in what is now Western Australia, which became known as the Swan River.
A belief backed by countless observations was undone by a single flock of birds.
Induction also fails when we generalise from too few cases, such as judging a whole city on one rude waiter.
Abduction: best explanation.
The American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce named a third kind, abduction.
It starts with a surprising observation and asks what would best explain it.
The lawn is wet this morning.
Did it rain, did the sprinkler run, or did dew form?
A bone-dry footpath points to the sprinkler.
This is also called inference to the best explanation, and it is what Holmes was really doing with Watson.
Doctors diagnosing from symptoms and mechanics tracing an engine noise do the same.
It is risky, because the best explanation you can think of may not be true: perhaps Watson was tanned from a holiday and hurt his arm falling off a horse.
Treating abduction as deduction is a known fallacy, affirming the consequent: ‘If it rained, the lawn would be wet.
The lawn is wet.
Therefore it rained.’
Using all three together.
In practice the three kinds of reasoning work as a team, and science is a good model.
A researcher notices something odd and uses abduction to propose a likely explanation, called a hypothesis.
They then use deduction to work out what should happen if that explanation is true: if this fertiliser helps plants grow, then plants given it should grow taller than identical plants without it.
Finally they gather observations and use induction to judge whether the evidence supports the idea.
Then the cycle starts again.
You can do the same with everyday puzzles.
When you land on an explanation, ask what else could explain the facts, what your idea predicts, and whether you've checked.
The key idea: Holmes's first meeting with Watson shows reasoning from small clues to a big conclusion, though not strictly deduction.
Part two. Correlation vs causation.
Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together.
Does ice cream kill?
The most useful idea for reading any headline.
Moving together.
A correlation means two things tend to change together.
As ice-cream sales rise, so do drownings.
Countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel Prizes per person.
People who carry lighters get lung cancer more often.
All of these correlations are real.
But in none of them does the first thing cause the second.
'Correlation doesn't imply causation' is one of the most important phrases in science, and one of the most ignored in headlines and advertising.
Hidden factors and flipped arrows.
Often a third factor, called a confounding variable, drives both things.
Hot weather makes people buy ice cream and go swimming, so drownings rise.
Wealthier countries eat more chocolate and also fund more research.
Smoking causes people to carry lighters and causes lung cancer.
Ask: is something causing both?
Sometimes the arrow points the other way.
People who use walking sticks tend to be less mobile, but the sticks don't cause it; poor mobility leads people to use sticks.
Do diet soft drinks cause weight gain, or are people already worried about their weight more likely to choose them?
Always consider whether the effect might be the cause.
Pure coincidence.
With enough data, some things line up by pure chance.
For about a decade, the number of films Nicolas Cage appeared in each year closely tracked the number of people who drowned by falling into US swimming pools.
Per capita cheese consumption tracked the number of people who died by becoming tangled in their bedsheets.
The writer Tyler Vigen collects these 'spurious correlations'.
If you compare enough random things, some will match beautifully while meaning nothing.
Observing and testing.
Many health headlines come from observational studies, where researchers observe what people do rather than assigning treatments.
They're valuable and sometimes the only ethical option: you can't randomly assign people to smoke.
But people who choose to do something differ in other ways.
Good studies adjust for known confounders like age, income and smoking, but unknown ones can still mislead.
The gold standard for cause and effect is the randomised controlled trial.
Participants are randomly assigned to groups, such as a new drug or a placebo.
Randomisation makes the groups similar in every way, including factors nobody measured, so the treatment is the only systematic difference.
Blinding, where people don't know their group, further reduces bias.
Building the case, reading headlines.
Sometimes causation can be shown without trials.

The link between smoking and lung cancer was proven by overwhelming evidence: it was very strong, appeared in study after study and different populations, more smoking meant more risk, quitting reduced it, smoking came first, and laboratory research showed how smoke damages cells.
Epidemiologist Austin Bradford Hill set out such criteria in 1965, and they're still used.
Headlines often turn correlations into causes: 'Coffee makes you live longer' when coffee drinkers merely lived longer.
Watch for 'causes', 'boosts', 'prevents'.
Ask: Was this an observational study or a randomised trial?
What else could explain the link?
Could the cause run the other way?
The key idea: A correlation means two things change together, which doesn't mean one causes the other.
Part three. How to spot misinformation.
False stories spread faster than true ones.
Professional fact-checkers use a few simple habits you can copy in 30 seconds.
Why falsehood spreads.
A major 2018 MIT study of millions of tweets found that false news spread further, faster and deeper than true news, and was about 70% more likely to be retweeted.
People, not bots, were mainly responsible.
False stories tend to be more novel and emotionally charged, triggering surprise, fear or disgust, which is what makes us share them.
If a post makes you instantly furious, frightened or triumphant, slow down.
Misleading content is often engineered to provoke emotion, because emotion bypasses careful thinking.
Watch especially for content that confirms what you already believe about people you disagree with.
The stronger your reaction, the more worth spending 30 seconds checking.
Mistakes and deception.
Misinformation is false or misleading information shared by people who believe it, like a relative forwarding a fake health tip.
Disinformation is false information spread deliberately to deceive, for profit, politics or to cause chaos.
There's also malinformation: true information used out of context to mislead, like an old photo presented as happening today.
Much of what spreads online is a mix: a kernel of truth wrapped in exaggeration or missing context.
It isn't only 'other people' who fall for it.
It's designed to exploit everyone's instincts.
SIFT and lateral reading.
Digital literacy expert Mike Caulfield developed a four-step method called SIFT.
Stop: pause before reacting or sharing.
Investigate the source: who's behind this, and what's their expertise and agenda?
Find better coverage: see what trusted outlets or fact-checkers say.
Trace claims, quotes and media to their original context.
Most checks take under a minute.
When Stanford researchers compared professional fact-checkers, historians and students evaluating websites, the fact-checkers were fastest and most accurate.
Their secret was lateral reading: rather than scrolling the site itself, they opened new tabs and searched for what others said about the source.
Professional-looking sites and official-sounding names are easy to fake.
What independent sources say is much harder to fake.
Images and fact-checkers.
Photos and videos are often real but taken out of context: an old flood picture reshared as a new disaster, or footage from another country.
A reverse image search, using tools like Google Lens or TinEye, can reveal where and when an image first appeared.
For video, screenshot a key frame and search that.
Clues like signs, shop names, number plates, weather and which side of the road cars drive on can confirm where it was taken.
Independent fact-checkers investigate viral claims and publish their evidence, including AAP FactCheck in Australia, and Full Fact and Snopes internationally.
Search the claim plus 'fact check'.
'Prebunking', learning manipulation techniques like fake experts and emotional language in advance, helps people resist misinformation.
You're doing that right now.
Talking to believers.
When friends or family share misinformation, mocking or lecturing usually backfires, making people defend their views harder.
It's more effective to stay curious and respectful: ask where they heard it and what would change their mind.
Share a reliable source privately rather than correcting them in public.
Explaining how a manipulation technique works can be more persuasive than arguing about the specific claim.
And model good behaviour yourself: when you share something that turns out to be false, correct it openly.
The key idea: False stories spread faster than true ones, driven by people responding to emotion rather than by bots.
Part four. Why conspiracy theories feel so convincing.
Real conspiracies happen, yet most grand theories about secret plots fall apart.
Learn why they grip clever people, and how to tell a real cover-up from a story.
Some conspiracies are real.
In 1972, burglars were caught inside the Democratic Party's offices in the Watergate building in Washington.
Over two years, journalists and investigators uncovered a cover-up that reached the White House, and President Richard Nixon resigned in 1974.
For decades, tobacco companies also played down what their own scientists knew about smoking's harms.
So powerful people sometimes collude and lie.
That is what makes conspiracy theories plausible.
The question isn't whether conspiracies ever happen.
It is how to tell real ones, uncovered through documents, whistleblowers and court cases, from the many theories that never produce solid evidence however long people look.
Why they feel true.
When something shocking happens, a small, random cause feels insulting.
Psychologists call this proportionality bias: a big effect seems to need a big explanation.
The 1963 assassination of John F.
Kennedy is a classic case.
A lone gunman changing history feels wrong, so a grand plot seems fitting.
Recognise when an explanation appeals mainly because it feels emotionally right.
Our ancestors who assumed a predator in a rustle in the grass were safer than those who assumed wind.
Many researchers think this shaped minds that over-detect patterns and intentions.
Conspiracy theories turn chaos into a story with villains and a plan.
That can be comforting, since someone is in charge.
People are more drawn to them when anxious, powerless or uncertain.
The self-sealing story.
Here is a warning sign worth memorising.
Ask a believer what evidence would change their mind.
If the answer is 'nothing', or every piece of contrary evidence is explained away as part of the plot, the theory has become self-sealing.
Missing evidence proves the cover-up.
Official denials prove the cover-up.
Experts who disagree are in on it.
This structure feels powerful because it can't be refuted, but that is exactly its weakness.
A claim that survives every possible observation tells you nothing about the world.
Real investigations work the other way.
Journalists who exposed Watergate could point to money trails, tapes and witnesses.
When a theory's main evidence is the absence of evidence, be cautious.
The problem of numbers.
The Apollo programme employed hundreds of thousands of people across government agencies, universities and private companies.
A hoax would have needed all of them, plus rival scientists in the Soviet Union who tracked the missions, to stay silent for over fifty years.
In 2016, physicist David Grimes published a model estimating how quickly large conspiracies would be likely to leak.
His rough conclusion was that secrets involving thousands of people tend to come out within a few years.
You don't need the maths to see the logic.
People talk, change jobs, write memoirs, fall out with their bosses and seek fame.
Real conspiracies usually involve small groups, and even those are often exposed eventually.
Motives and talking it through.
Ask not only who benefits from the alleged plot but who benefits from you believing it.
Some promoters sell supplements, courses or subscriptions.
Others earn advertising money, and outrage keeps people watching.
Some foreign governments have spread divisive stories to weaken trust in other countries' institutions.
None of this proves a claim false, but apply scepticism evenly, to governments and corporations and to influencers telling you what they are hiding.
If someone you care about is deep in a rabbit hole, mockery backfires.
Ask genuine questions: what first made you think this, and what would change your mind?
Find common ground and share your own uncertainty.
Prebunking, such as Cambridge's online games, teaches manipulation tricks in advance.
People rarely leave a belief by losing an argument, but often return through trusted friends.
The key idea: Real conspiracies happen, but they are uncovered through documents, whistleblowers and court cases, not by theories that never produce solid evidence.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which kind of reasoning was Holmes mostly using when he guessed Watson had been in Afghanistan?
Answer. Abduction.
Question two. What does 'correlation doesn't imply causation' mean?
Answer. Linked trends need not be cause and effect.
Question three. Why do false stories tend to spread faster than true ones?
Answer. They're novel and emotional, so people share them.
Question four. How are real conspiracies usually uncovered?
Answer. Through documents, whistleblowers and court cases.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
